title: Claude Code Hooks: I Tried to Get Past Them
summary: Claude Code hooks can block a tool call before it runs. We tested what a PreToolUse hook sees, where it fails open, and who can turn it off.
body_markdown:
In November 2025 Drew Gregory wrote about[allowlisting Bash commands in Claude Code](https://www.formal.ai/blog/allowlisting-bash-commands/) . Once` go test` ,` make` or` pnpm run` can run without a prompt, along with file edits, Claude Code can run any command, and a file watcher such as` next dev --turbopack` runs edited code with no Bash call at all. That post ended by recommending a sandbox.


The obvious next question is whether a` PreToolUse` hook closes those gaps.


Claude Code hooks are handlers that Claude Code runs at fixed points in a session: shell commands, HTTP endpoints, MCP tool calls, LLM prompts or subagents, in[Anthropic’s definition](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks) . A` PreToolUse` hook runs after Claude has written a tool call and before Claude Code executes it, and it can allow the call, deny it, ask you, or rewrite its arguments, which makes it the natural place for guardrails.


This post puts a` PreToolUse` hook in front of the same bypasses, checks what happens when a hook fails, and looks at who can switch hooks off.


The hook stopped every command whose danger was in the string it read, and missed every one where the danger lived somewhere else, in` package.json` , a Go test, a file a dev server loaded, or a spelling its pattern didn’t expect. When it broke, it failed open without a word in the session, and one line in a project’s settings switched it off along with the hooks in our own user settings.


We ran everything on Claude Code 2.1.319, macOS 26.7.1 on an Apple M5 Max, in headless` claude -p` sessions inside a throwaway repository, in` default` permission mode with the sandbox off unless a test says otherwise. Each run allowed the tool under test with` --allowedTools` , so the hook was the only thing in the way. A headless session can’t show a prompt, so where Claude Code would have asked, the transcript records a denial and its reason.


## What are Claude Code hooks?


Hooks in Claude Code are handlers you register in a settings file against a named event. Each handler has one of five types:` command` ,` http` ,` mcp_tool` ,` prompt` or` agent` , and Anthropic says agent hooks “are experimental and may change”. The[hooks reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#hook-lifecycle) lists 33 events as of November 2026, from` SessionStart` through` SessionEnd` , and a matcher on each hook narrows which tool or source it fires for.


A hook can live in` ~/.claude/settings.json` for every project, in a project’s` .claude/settings.json` (which is meant to be committed), in` .claude/settings.local.json` , in managed settings an admin controls, in a plugin’s` hooks/hooks.json` , or in the front matter of a skill or subagent. None of them replaces another: “Hook entries merge across settings levels rather than replacing each other.” The hooks you wrote and the hooks a repository ships run side by side.


### The Claude Code hook events that matter for security


Most of the events are about automation: notifications, compaction, worktrees, model switches. Six decide what a hook can do about a risky action:


Event When it fires What the hook can do


` PreToolUse` Before a tool call executes Allow, deny, ask or defer the call, or rewrite its input


` PermissionRequest` When a tool call needs a permission decision Allow or deny the request; deny and ask rules still apply


` PostToolUse` After a tool call succeeds Add a note or replace the output Claude sees; the tool has already run


` ConfigChange` When a configuration file changes during a session Block the change from applying to the session, except` policy_settings`


` FileChanged` When a watched file changes on disk Nothing: it runs after the write and has no decision control


` SessionStart` When a session begins or resumes Runs before any tool call, including in a repository you just cloned


The other 27 are in Anthropic’s full events list in the[hooks reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#hook-lifecycle) , and the[hooks guide](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide) walks through setting up the common ones.


## How a PreToolUse hook blocks a command


A command hook gets the event as JSON on stdin. For a Bash call,` tool_name` is` Bash` and` tool_input.command` holds the command string exactly as Claude wrote it, next to common fields such as` session_id` ,` cwd` and` permission_mode` .


Our baseline is two handlers on` Bash` in the project’s` .claude/settings.json` . The first runs only for commands that match` Bash(rm *)` ; the second reads every command:


```text
{
"hooks"  : {
"PreToolUse"  : [
{
"matcher"  :   "Bash"  ,
"hooks"  : [
{
"type"  :   "command"  ,
"if"  :   "Bash(rm *)"  ,
"command"  :   "/path/to/project/.claude/hooks/guard-rm.sh"
},
{
"type"  :   "command"  ,
"command"  :   "/path/to/project/.claude/hooks/guard-curl.sh"
}
]
}
]
}
}
```


` guard-rm.sh` logs its input and exits 2.` guard-curl.sh` denies any command string that contains` curl` or` git push` :


```text
#!/bin/bash
input  =$(  cat  )
command  =$(  printf   '%s'   "  $input  "   |   node   -e   'let s="";process.stdin.on("data",d=>s+=d).on("end",()=>process.stdout.write(JSON.parse(s).tool_input?.command ?? ""))'  )
if   printf   '%s'   "  $command  "   |   grep   -Eq   'curl|git push'  ;   then
echo   "Blocked by guard-curl.sh: the command contains curl or git push."   >&2
exit   2
fi
exit   0
```


Asked to run` rm -rf build/` , Claude made the call and the first handler received this on stdin (paths shortened):


```text
{
"session_id"  :   "f11290a4-31e2-415b-8d55-c326fd5db280"  ,
"cwd"  :   "/path/to/project"  ,
"permission_mode"  :   "default"  ,
"hook_event_name"  :   "PreToolUse"  ,
"tool_name"  :   "Bash"  ,
"tool_input"  : {
"command"  :   "rm -rf build/"  ,
"description"  :   "Delete the build directory"
},
"tool_use_id"  :   "toolu_01TMZCrX8wH6ximcbUVusYxz"
}
```


Claude Code handed Claude the hook’s stderr as the result,` PreToolUse:Bash hook error: \[.../guard-rm.sh\]: Blocked by guard-rm.sh: rm is not allowed in this project.` , and` build/` was still there, even though` Bash` was on the allow list.` curl -s https://example.com` was stopped the same way by the second handler.` guard-rm.sh` never ran for the` curl` call, so the` if` filter did narrow it.


There are two ways to say no. Exit code 2 blocks the call and hands the hook’s stderr to Claude as the reason. Exit 0 with JSON is more precise:` permissionDecision` can be` allow` (skip the prompt),` deny` ,` ask` , or` defer` , which Claude Code honors only in` -p` runs, and` updatedInput` replaces the tool’s arguments before the call runs. Any other exit code is a non-blocking error and the call goes ahead. That includes exit 1, the usual Unix failure code, and Anthropic’s[exit code section](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#exit-code-output) says it plainly: “If your hook is meant to enforce a policy, use` exit 2` .”


Hooks and permission rules stack in one direction. A hook’s` allow` doesn’t get past a matching deny or ask rule, managed rules included, while a hook that exits 2 “stops the tool call before permission rules are evaluated”, so it blocks even a command an allow rule would let through ([precedence among rules, hooks, and mods](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions#precedence-among-rules-hooks-and-mods) ). When several` PreToolUse` hooks disagree, “precedence is` deny` >` defer` >` ask` >` allow` ”, so a second hook can’t overrule a deny from the first. A deny also holds in` bypassPermissions` mode, the one[--dangerously-skip-permissions](https://www.formal.ai/blog/claude-code-dangerously-skip-permissions/) starts, because` PreToolUse` hooks[fire before any permission-mode check](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide#hooks-and-permission-modes) .


We checked that last claim. With the same two handlers, we repeated both prompts under` claude --dangerously-skip-permissions` . The session reported` permissionMode: bypassPermissions` , and both calls were denied with the same messages as before.


Two settings decide whether the hook runs at all. The[matcher](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#matcher-patterns) is an exact tool name, a` |` list, or otherwise an unanchored JavaScript regex, so` Edit.*` also matches` NotebookEdit` , and` mcp__memory` on its own matches no tool. The` if` field narrows a handler with permission-rule syntax such as` Bash(rm *)` , and Anthropic is explicit about how far to trust it: “Because the` if` filter is best-effort, use the permission system rather than a hook to enforce a hard allow or deny.”


## Testing a PreToolUse hook against the allowlisting bypasses


Anthropic’s permissions page has a list of[commands a Bash rule doesn’t match](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions#bash-rule-limits) : a deny on` Bash(curl *)` doesn’t stop` /usr/bin/curl` or` sh -c 'curl ...'` , and wrappers such as` npx` and` docker exec` “execute their arguments as a command”. For checks on the command itself, the same page points to hooks: “To inspect the full command text with your own logic before it runs, use a PreToolUse hook.” The tests below hand that hook the bypasses from the allowlisting post, where the command Claude asks to run and the code that ends up running are different things.


### ` npm test`


The` test` script in` package.json` decides what` npm test` executes, and changing it is an ordinary file edit for Claude.


With the` curl` handler in place and` npm test` and` Edit` allowed, we asked Claude to change the` test` script to` curl -s https://example.com | grep -o "<title>.*</title>"` and run` npm test` . The hook fired once, for the` npm test` call, and its input held` "command": "npm test"` and nothing about` curl` . It didn’t fire on the edit to` package.json` , because its matcher is` Bash` . The test printed` <title>Example Domain</title>` , so the request left the machine.


### ` go test`


A Go test can start any process with` exec.Command` . It was the first bypass in the allowlisting post.


Same hook, with` go test` and` Write` allowed. Claude wrote` add_test.go` with a test that runs` exec.Command("curl", "-s", "https://example.com")` and logs the output, then ran` go test -v ./...` . The hook saw` go test -v ./... 2>&1` and let it through, and the test log contained the page’s` <title>Example Domain</title>` .


### ` next dev --turbopack`


A watcher that the developer started runs edited code without Claude making a Bash call. A` FileChanged` hook can see the file change, but Anthropic’s reference says it runs “after the change” with no decision control, so it “can’t block the write”.


We started` next dev --turbopack` (Next.js 16.4.5) ourselves, loaded an API route once, then asked Claude, with only` Read` and` Edit` allowed, to add the allowlisting post’s snippet to the top of that route: an` execSync` call, here running` curl` and saving the page to a file. A logging hook on every tool recorded four events:` PreToolUse` and` PostToolUse` for` Read` , then for` Edit` . No Bash call happened. Saving the file alone didn’t run the code; the next request to the route did, and the saved page held` <title>Example Domain</title>` . Any request is enough: a browser tab, a test or a health check.


### ` /usr/bin/curl` ,` sh -c` and` git -C`


A hook that reads the command string has to understand shell, and Anthropic’s own table of what a Bash rule misses works as a test list. One published set of guards is karanb192’s[claude-code-hooks](https://github.com/karanb192/claude-code-hooks) , whose` block-dangerous-commands` hook targets commands such as` rm -rf ~` , fork bombs and` curl | sh` .


We ran six command forms, each in its own session, against two guards: the grep-style` guard-curl.sh` from above, and two` if` filters,` Bash(curl *)` and` Bash(git push *)` , in front of a script that denies whatever reaches it. Every hook received the command exactly as Claude was asked to write it.


Command Grep hook` if` filters


` /usr/bin/curl -s https://example.com` Blocked Ran


` sh -c 'curl -s https://example.com'` Blocked Ran


` URL=https://example.com && curl -s $URL` Blocked Blocked


` git -C . push` Ran Ran


` git -c push.default=current push` Ran Ran


` git 'push' origin main` Ran Blocked


The grep hook missed all three pushes because none of them contains the substring` git push` . The` if` filters read past the` URL=` assignment and the quotes around` 'push'` , but matched neither a full path nor a command inside` sh -c` , the two gaps Anthropic’s table warns about. The pushes that ran only failed because our test repository had no remote: git printed` fatal: No configured push destination.`


karanb192’s guard has a different job. At commit` 57a28c7` (2026-10-17), its default` high` level matches regular expressions for patterns such as` curl` or` wget` piped into` sh` or` bash` , force pushes to` main` or` master` , and` rm` aimed at the home directory, root or system paths. None of the six forms above is on its list, so it let all six through. Against its own patterns, it caught` curl ... | sh` ,` /usr/bin/curl ... | bash` ,` git push --force origin main` ,` git push -f origin HEAD:main` and` rm -rf ~` . It missed` curl ... | /bin/sh` ,` curl ... | zsh` ,` sh -c "$(curl ...)"` ,` bash <(curl ...)` ,` git -C . push --force origin main` ,` git 'push' --force origin main` and` rm -rf $HOME/` . Installed as a hook, it denied` git push --force origin main` with` ⛔ \[git-force-main\] force push to main/master` and let` git -C . push --force origin main` run. That isn’t a flaw peculiar to one project: any guard that pattern-matches the command string has the same edge.


## When a hook fails open


By default, a broken hook stops nothing. Anthropic’s list of non-blocking errors covers a hook that exits with any code other than 0 or 2, one that doesn’t start, and one that prints invalid JSON, and in each case “The action goes ahead.” A mistyped script path is the quiet version of this: “a mistyped path in` settings.json` means the hook never runs.”


Timeouts behave the same way. Command, HTTP and MCP tool hooks get 600 seconds by default (30 on` UserPromptSubmit` ), and on` PreToolUse` , “a timed-out` command` ,` http` , or` mcp_tool` hook doesn’t block the tool call”, so Anthropic’s advice is “don’t count on a stalled hook to act as a gate”. A hook that hands its decision to a background process and exits loses it too: a deny that process prints after Claude Code has stopped reading “doesn’t block the tool call”. HTTP hooks treat non-2xx responses and connection failures as non-blocking errors.


The fix is one field.["onFailure": "block"](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#block-the-action-when-a-hook-fails) on a` command` or` http` hook makes a failed hook block the action. It requires Claude Code v2.1.295 or later and has no effect on async hooks.


We pointed the` curl` handler at a misspelled script path, then at a script that sleeps 20 seconds under a 3-second` timeout` , each with and without` onFailure` , and asked Claude to run` curl -s https://example.com` :


Hook Without` onFailure` With` "onFailure": "block"`


Misspelled script path` curl` ran and printed` 200` Blocked:` failed; blocking because onFailure is "block"`


Sleeps past a 3-second timeout` curl` ran and printed` 200` Blocked:` timed out; blocking because onFailure is "block"`


The broken hook left no trace in the session: nothing in the transcript, and Claude reported a clean run. Only the` claude --debug` log had it:` Hook PreToolUse:Bash (PreToolUse) error: status code 127` , followed by` No such file or directory` .


## Who can turn a hook off?


Anyone who can change the settings that load it, and in some modes that includes Claude. Command hooks “execute shell commands with your full user permissions” according to Anthropic’s[security considerations](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#security-considerations) , and they run outside the Claude Code sandbox, as we covered in the[sandbox post](https://www.formal.ai/blog/claude-code-sandbox/) . A hook protects the machine only while its configuration and its script stay as written, and there are three ways for that to change.


### Claude editing its own settings


` .claude/` is a[protected path](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes#protected-paths) , along with` .git` ,` .vscode` ,` .idea` and a few others. Writes to it are prompted in` default` and` acceptEdits` mode, sent to the classifier in` auto` , denied in` dontAsk` and allowed in` bypassPermissions` . Allow rules don’t change that. The prompt itself has a wider option, though, “Yes, and allow Claude to edit files in this project’s .claude folder for this session”, and after one click the rest of the session’s edits to project hooks go through unasked. Sandboxed shell commands can’t write the` .claude` settings files,` .claude/hooks` or the hooks inside` .git` either, because “A command that could edit those files could grant itself permissions, or add a hook or MCP server that Claude Code runs outside the sandbox.”


That leaves two cases the docs don’t settle: a guard script stored outside` .claude/` , and a settings file written by code Claude runs rather than by Claude’s Edit tool.` ConfigChange` adds a third question. A` "decision": "block"` “prevents the configuration change from being applied” to the running session; the reference doesn’t say what happens to the file on disk.


We tested all three, plus the protected path itself, with` Edit` on the allow list:


- **Claude removing the hook .** Asked to set` "hooks"` to` {}` in` .claude/settings.json` , Claude was stopped in` default` and` acceptEdits` mode with` Claude requested permissions to write to .../.claude/settings.json, but you haven't granted it yet.` The allow rule didn’t open it. In` auto` mode the classifier let the edit through in three runs out of three, and` bypassPermissions` allowed it. We asked for the edit directly, so the classifier was judging the user’s own request. We didn’t test an instruction planted in a file.
- **A guard outside` .claude/` .** With the hook pointing at` scripts/guard.sh` , Claude removed its` exit 2` in` default` and` acceptEdits` mode with no prompt. Outside` .claude/` , a guard script is an ordinary file, and the same allow rule that` .claude/` ignored covered it.
- **A test rewriting the settings .** A` test.js` that overwrites` .claude/settings.json` with` {"hooks":{}}` did exactly that under` npm test` with the sandbox off. With the sandbox on, the write failed with` EPERM: operation not permitted, open '.claude/settings.json'` . When we asked Claude to write that test itself, it did in one run; in the next, Anthropic’s safeguards flagged the identical request and Claude declined, so we put the file in place ourselves and asked Claude only to run` npm test` .
- **` ConfigChange` with` "decision": "block"` .** The hook fired when Claude emptied` "hooks"` , and the running session kept the old ones: the next` rm -rf build/` was still denied. The edit was on disk all the same, and the next session loaded the empty file and ran` rm -rf build/` . Without the` ConfigChange` hook, the change applied to the running session at once, and` rm` went through in the same session.


### A repository’s` disableAllHooks`


[disableAllHooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#disable-or-remove-hooks) follows settings precedence, so “a` "disableAllHooks": false` in a project’s` .claude/settings.json` overrides a` true` in your user settings.” The reference shows that direction only. Whether a project’s` true` also silences the hooks in your user settings isn’t stated, so we checked. Managed hooks are out of reach either way: only` disableAllHooks` set in managed settings can disable them, and “There is no way to disable an individual hook while keeping it in the configuration.”


It does. We put an` rm` guard in` ~/.claude/settings.json` . In a project with empty settings, it denied` rm -rf build/` . In a project whose` .claude/settings.json` held only` { "disableAllHooks": true }` , the user hook never ran and` build/` was deleted. A repository you clone can switch off the guards you set for every project. A hook you depend on belongs in managed settings, covered below.


### Cloned repositories and` claude -p`


In an interactive session, Claude Code “holds back hooks from every settings file, including your own` ~/.claude/settings.json` , until you accept the workspace trust dialog”. A` -p` or SDK session is different: “Claude Code never shows the dialog and treats the folder as trusted, so hooks committed in a repository’s` .claude/settings.json` run in a folder you’ve never trusted.” Before scripting` claude -p` over a repository you didn’t write, Anthropic suggests reviewing its` .claude/` settings, starting with` --bare` , or passing` --settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}'` ([workspace trust](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#workspace-trust) ).


We cloned a repository whose` .claude/settings.json` has one` SessionStart` hook,` touch /tmp/hook-ran` , into a folder Claude Code had never opened.` claude -p "hello"` created` /tmp/hook-ran` . With` --settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}'` , Claude answered and the file didn’t appear.


## Five Claude Code hooks worth running


Hooks are still the cheapest place in Claude Code to stop an obvious mistake and tell Claude why. These examples are worth the setup, as long as you know what each one misses:


1. A` PreToolUse` hook on` Bash` that denies destructive commands, such as` rm -rf` outside the project and force pushes. It reads the command string, so whatever got past` guard-curl.sh` in the tests above gets past this too.
2. A hook on` Read|Edit|Write` and` Bash` that denies` .env` ,` .git/` and key files, in line with Anthropic’s “Skip sensitive files” advice. Files you mention with` @` in a prompt are added “without any tool call”, so no` PreToolUse` hook fires for them.
3. A` git push` guard for protected branches.` git -C . push` and` git -c push.default=current push` are the forms to test it against: in our runs, both got past a grep for` git push` and an` if: "Bash(git push *)"` filter.
4. A` ConfigChange` hook on` project_settings` and` local_settings` that logs every change and blocks the ones you care about. It can’t block` policy_settings` , and it doesn’t run for server-managed settings.
5. An async` PostToolUse` hook that appends each tool call to a log. It can’t block anything, since the tool has already run, and it records only what passes through Claude’s tools.


Every blocking hook in that list should deny with exit 2 or JSON rather than exit 1, set` "onFailure": "block"` , and run a script by absolute path. Anthropic’s[hook security best practices](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#security-considerations) add “Always quote shell variables” and “Block path traversal”.


We wrote all five as small Node scripts and ran them together on Claude Code 2.1.319. The blocking ones return a JSON` deny` :


```text
{
"hooks"  : {
"PreToolUse"  : [
{
"matcher"  :   "Bash"  ,
"hooks"  : [
{
"type"  :   "command"  ,
"command"  :   "node /path/to/project/.claude/hooks/block-destructive.js"  ,
"onFailure"  :   "block"
},
{
"type"  :   "command"  ,
"command"  :   "node /path/to/project/.claude/hooks/guard-push.js"  ,
"onFailure"  :   "block"
}
]
},
{
"matcher"  :   "Read|Edit|Write|Bash"  ,
"hooks"  : [
{
"type"  :   "command"  ,
"command"  :   "node /path/to/project/.claude/hooks/block-sensitive.js"  ,
"onFailure"  :   "block"
}
]
}
],
"ConfigChange"  : [
{
"matcher"  :   "project_settings|local_settings"  ,
"hooks"  : [
{
"type"  :   "command"  ,
"command"  :   "node /path/to/project/.claude/hooks/config-guard.js"
}
]
}
],
"PostToolUse"  : [
{
"matcher"  :   "*"  ,
"hooks"  : [
{
"type"  :   "command"  ,
"command"  :   "node /path/to/project/.claude/hooks/audit-log.js"  ,
"async"  :   true
}
]
}
]
}
}
```


Each one did its job and had the gap the list predicts:


1. ` block-destructive.js` resolves every` rm -r` or` rm -f` target against the project directory. It denied` rm -rf /tmp/...` and` rm -rf ~/...` , and a` git push --force` .` cd /tmp && rm -rf hooks-lab-victim` deleted the folder, because the script resolved the relative path against the project, and` find ... -delete` never mentions` rm` .
2. ` block-sensitive.js` denied reading` .env` and` .git/config` and running` cat .env` .` cat .en*` printed the key, and` cat .e""nv` got past the script when we fed it that command directly. Asked about` @.env` , Claude answered with the key and no hook ran at all.
3. ` guard-push.js` strips quotes and also denies any push while` main` is checked out, which caught` git -C . push` ,` git -c push.default=current push` ,` git 'push' origin main` and` sh -c "git push origin main"` . A git alias,` git ship origin main` with` ship` set to` push` , went through; it failed only because our test repository had no remote.
4. ` config-guard.js` received` "source": "local_settings"` when Claude created` .claude/settings.local.json` with no hooks, and blocked it: the next` rm -rf /tmp/...` in that session was still denied. The file itself was still written, as in the earlier` ConfigChange` test.
5. ` audit-log.js` logged every call that succeeded. Calls a hook denied, and a push that failed, never reached` PostToolUse` , so the log only records what ran. What Claude tried and was refused is in the session transcript.


## Claude Code managed settings for hooks


On a team, the hooks that hold are the ones developers can’t edit. Managed settings sit at the top of[settings precedence](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings#settings-precedence) , above` --settings` , local project, shared project and user settings. The file is` /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json` on macOS,` /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json` on Linux and WSL, and` C:\\Program Files\\ClaudeCode\\managed-settings.json` on Windows, or it arrives through MDM or server-managed settings ([managed settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-settings) ).


The hook-related keys, from the[settings reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#allowmanagedhooksonly) :


- ` allowManagedHooksOnly: true` : “only managed hooks run, plus Agent SDK hooks and hooks from plugins your managed settings force-enable”.
- ` strictPluginOnlyCustomization` , set to` true` or to` \["hooks"\]` , blocks hooks from user and project sources so they can come only from plugins or managed settings.
- ` disableAllHooks` in managed settings is the only switch that turns managed hooks off.
- ` allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly` makes managed settings the only source of allow, ask and deny rules, which settles the other half of the precedence question.
- ` allowedHttpHookUrls` limits which URLs HTTP hooks can call, and` httpHookAllowedEnvVars` limits which environment variables they can put in request headers.


Anthropic names two limits on the same page. “A developer who is an administrator on the machine can edit the managed source itself”, and “managed settings bind Claude Code only. A developer who calls the API from another tool isn’t under them.” To confirm a machine picked the file up, run` /status` : its` Setting sources` line shows` Enterprise managed settings (file)` , the older name many guides still use for Claude Code enterprise settings.


## Checking the process instead of the command with Formal Endpoint


The bypasses that got past the hook have one thing in common: the hook reads the command Claude wrote, and the network request comes from a process that command started.[Formal Endpoint](https://www.formal.ai/products/endpoint/) , the egress proxy we build, works from the other end. In[Transparent Mode](https://docs.formal.ai/docs/guides/client-apps/desktop-app#transparent-mode) it captures TCP connections at the OS network layer, and on macOS it knows which process opened each one and that process’s ancestors.


A[network rule](https://docs.formal.ai/docs/guides/network-rules) picks the connections the Endpoint handles. Each rule is a CEL expression with a condition for` pre_tcp` ,` pre_tls` and` post_tls` .` process.has_agent_ancestor` is “True when the connecting process is a known agent or has one in its ancestor list”, so a` curl` started by` npm test` , started in turn by Claude Code, matches however the command line was written. The starting rule in the docs:


```text
{
"condition"  : {
"pre_tcp"  : process.is_agent || process.has_agent_ancestor,
"pre_tls"  :   true  ,
"post_tls"  : technology in [  "mcp"  ,   "llm"  ]
}
}
```


` pre_tcp` runs on macOS only, where Claude Code is identified by its code signature. Linux has no signature check: the agent flags compare process names, so there Claude Code is the process called` claude` .


The` next dev` case is where that stops. A watcher the developer started in their own terminal has no agent ancestor, so an agent rule doesn’t match the code it runs, even when Claude wrote that code. Covering it takes a rule on the destination for every process, or the sandbox or a VM around the whole session.


The closest thing Formal has to a` PreToolUse` check sits on the model’s response. Our[Protect Git Tokens in Command Lines](https://docs.formal.ai/docs/guides/example-use-cases/protect-git-tokens-in-command-lines) guide is a` response` policy on LLM traffic that “blocks agent tool calls whose arguments contain a token or a URL with credentials, so the command never runs”. The Endpoint evaluates it. No settings file in a repository can turn it off, because it isn’t in one. The guide is direct about its reach: “The patterns match common formats, not every secret. A token passed through a credential helper, a script file, or a variable outside a URL does not match.”


Two more documented controls cover what a hook can’t take back.[Credential injection](https://docs.formal.ai/docs/guides/example-use-cases/keep-stripe-api-keys-off-laptops) keeps the key off the laptop: a Formal Connector stores it and adds it to requests on their way upstream, and in the Stripe guide’s words, “Stripe receives the real key. The laptop never does.” A test file has nothing to read. The[proxies post](https://www.formal.ai/blog/using-proxies-claude-code/) applies the same setup to the Anthropic API key. And the[block agent git pushes](https://docs.formal.ai/docs/guides/example-use-cases/block-agent-git-pushes) guide blocks` git-receive-pack` from Claude Code’s process tree while a push from your own terminal goes through.


The limits are the Endpoint’s own. Process identity from code signatures is macOS only, and Linux matches process names. Transparent Mode isn’t available on Windows, where the Endpoint connects through` formal connect` only. Agent rules only know the agents in Formal’s identity list, so an agent missing from it passes through them.[AI coding agent security](https://www.formal.ai/use-cases/ai-coding-agent-security/) covers how the same rules apply to Cursor, Codex and Devin, and our guide to[egress filtering](https://www.formal.ai/academy/egress-filtering/) covers the rules underneath.


## What we’d run


- Hooks for the mistakes an agent makes in plain sight, and for telling Claude why it was stopped.
- Deny with exit 2 or a JSON` deny` , never exit 1, and` "onFailure": "block"` on every blocking hook.
- Scripts by absolute path, kept inside` .claude/hooks` . Outside it, our guard was an ordinary file Claude edited without a prompt.
- A look at a repository’s` .claude/settings.json` before working in it: its` disableAllHooks` switched off our user hooks too.
- Team hooks from managed settings, with` allowManagedHooksOnly` .
- ` --bare` or` --settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}'` for` claude -p` on repositories nobody reviewed.
- The sandbox or a VM around the session, and egress and credentials handled outside the agent.


Asked for the safest way to run Claude Code, Anthropic’s[security page](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/security) recommends VMs “to run scripts and make tool calls, especially when interacting with external web services”, and reminds readers that no system is “completely immune to all attacks”. For what Formal adds around the agent on a team, see[Claude Code security](https://www.formal.ai/integrations/claude-code/) .


Hooks earned a place in our setup as the cheapest way to stop Claude’s obvious mistakes and tell it why. They didn’t earn trust as a boundary: everything that got past ours moved the dangerous part somewhere the hook doesn’t look, and the settings that load a hook could be changed by a repository, by Claude in` auto` mode, or by a test. Keep the hooks, and put the checks you can’t afford to lose outside the agent, where no settings file can turn them off.


## Frequently asked questions


### What’s the difference between PreToolUse and PostToolUse hooks?


A` PreToolUse` hook runs before the tool call and can stop it. A` PostToolUse` hook runs after a call succeeds: its` "decision": "block"` only adds a reason next to the tool result, and` updatedToolOutput` replaces the output Claude sees. Failed calls go to` PostToolUseFailure` instead, and` PostToolBatch` fires once a batch of parallel calls has resolved, before the next model call.


### How do I see which Claude Code hooks are active?


Type` /hooks` . It opens a read-only browser that labels each hook with where it comes from (user, project or local settings, a plugin, or the current session) and shows what it runs and which file defines it. To change a hook, edit that file; there’s no per-hook off switch. To watch hooks as they run, start a session with` claude --debug` .


### Can hooks be written in something other than bash?


Yes. Besides` command` hooks, Claude Code supports` http` hooks, which POST the event JSON to a URL,` mcp_tool` hooks,` prompt` hooks that ask a model, and experimental` agent` hooks that spawn a subagent with tools such as Read and Grep. On Windows, a command hook can run in PowerShell with` "shell": "powershell"` .


### Can a hook block a command in dangerously-skip-permissions mode?


Yes. A` PreToolUse` hook that returns a deny “blocks the tool even in` bypassPermissions` mode or with` --dangerously-skip-permissions` ”. What changes in that mode is the protected-path check: writes to` .claude/` , where project hooks live, are allowed without a prompt. The[dangerously-skip-permissions post](https://www.formal.ai/blog/claude-code-dangerously-skip-permissions/) covers what else the mode turns off.


### Do Claude Code hooks run inside the sandbox?


No. Anthropic’s[sandboxing page](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#what-runs-outside-the-sandbox) says “The sandbox covers shell commands only. Claude’s file tools, MCP servers, and hooks run outside it.” The sandbox does protect hooks from sandboxed commands: they can’t write` .claude/hooks` or the hooks inside` .git` , so a sandboxed test can’t plant one there.


### Can an HTTP hook send session data to an outside service?


It sends its event to whatever URL it’s configured with. Once` allowedHttpHookUrls` is set, Claude Code “runs an HTTP hook only if its URL matches one of the patterns and blocks the rest without running them”, and` httpHookAllowedEnvVars` caps which environment variables any HTTP hook can put in its headers. Both are arrays that merge across settings files, so the list in effect combines every file’s entries.
